newsitem.title: GERMANY: German CDU expects Kohl to run again in 1998.
newsitem.headline: German CDU expects Kohl to run again in 1998.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's allies expect him to run for re-election next year after he gave an emotional speech to a closed meeting of his Christian Democrats (CDU), a key aide said on Wednesday.

Rudolf Seiters, the CDU's deputy parliamentary leader and one of Kohl's closest confidants, said parliamentarians reacted with thunderous applause on Tuesday evening when Kohl, 66, declared to them: "I know my duty."

Already 14 years in office, Kohl has kept Germany guessing despite repeated calls for him to run. Many CDU allies say a clear decision to run would help him get over a popularity drop prompted by record unemployment and feuds in his coalition.

"The parliamentary faction and the party want, hope, expect and also assume that Helmut Kohl will run again," Seiters told North German Radio. "The applause yesterday evening from the deputies expressed this very clearly."

Other officials said some deputies had tears in their eyes listening to Kohl, who has been under fire from younger CDU leaders for not showing enough leadership in Bonn's efforts to reform its tax system and qualify for Europe's single currency.
"The mood has has changed in Kohl's favour," one said.
Kohl, who hinted last week he might reconsider his future after June's European Union summit in Amsterdam, told his party he would not be forced into a decision before he was ready.
But he added that he had a responsibility to the party and the centre-right coalition and said: "I know my duty."
Many in the CDU were dismayed last week after he introduced a fresh note of uncertainty at a time when the coalition was under more pressure than at any time since the 1994 election.

A wave of criticism from within the party at the way reform projects were being mismanaged led editorialists to write that Kohl was losing his legendary grip over internal dissent and might not have the authority and new ideas now required.

Italina Prime Minister Romano Prodi joined the chorus on Monday, saying Germany's problems now were more political than economic and that Bonn had to take tough decisions to ensure it qualified for the EU's economic and monetary union (EMU).
The chancellor, a master of 'sitting out' his difficulties, probably has to announce his decision by the CDU's annual congress in October at the latest.
By that time unemployment -- which leaped by a staggering half a million last month -- should have receded a little, and the reforms could have taken shape.
Bonn's rumour mill says he might announce his decision in early April, after he returns from his annual Easter slimming vacation in Austria.
The hefty chancellor often returns from the two weeks of dieting on bread rolls and water with plans to retake the initiative in domestic politics.

His CDU is now level with the opposition Social Democrats at 37 percent support each. But his Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partner languishes around six percent while the SPD's potential ally, the ecologist Greens, stand at around 11 percent.
But Kohl, an often diffident leader who comes alive when elections loom, was even further behind in the polls one year before the last two elections and won both contests.
